paragraphs: I was allowed to do a clerkship for three months from April at St.Olavs Hospital, the hospital attached to the Norwegian University of Science and Technology. This university became a partner school of Nagoya University this year. With curiosity about wanting to go somewhere nobody had gone, and from seeing photos of the nature-rich city of Trondheim, I decided without hesitation to go to Norway. I had no prior information and was a little anxious about doing the clerkship alone, but I fondly remember departing with a heart full of anticipation about being able to live for three months in Norway, a place I might not even go to on a trip. I would like to introduce my clerkship life as the first Nagoya University student to go to Norway.

It is located in a city called Trondheim, about an hour by plane from Oslo, the capital of Norway. It is the largest public university in Norway. St.Olavs Hospital, the attached hospital, has 1,366 beds and is responsible for the medical care of Trøndelag County, with a population of 280,000. A ward building is built for each clinical department, and I was impressed by the sight of people using scooters to move around inside the hospital.

I rotated through vascular surgery, orthopedic surgery and gastrointestinal surgery, one month each. The official language of Norway is Norwegian, but almost everyone can speak English. Conferences, history taking and charts are all in Norwegian, but in every department the doctors were truly kind and explained a lot in English, before patients came to the outpatient clinic and even during surgery.

The first, vascular surgery, was small with only about 10 doctors and had a homelike atmosphere. The conference every morning from 7:45 felt like listening to Norwegian sutra chanting for about an hour, and honestly I found it quite boring until I got used to it, and I was often laughed at afterward with "You don't understand anything!", but since I thought that in a clerkship abroad no one pays attention to you unless you speak up yourself, thanks to the doctors who always looked out for me, I was able to keep going without ever oversleeping. Unlike clerkships in Japan, no clerkship schedule for students is arranged, so every day I was asked "How is yourplan today?" and decided myself whether to go to the outpatient clinic, join surgery, or go observe another department. In the outpatient clinic, the room for looking at charts and the room for examining are separate, unlike in Japan they do not take the history while writing the chart, and each person was given about 20 minutes for the history alone, and I was impressed that they valued communication with patients very much. Also, in the gaps between patients, several doctors searched for Japan and Nagoya University Hospital on the chart computer, or we showed each other where we lived on Google Maps, and I was happy that they welcomed me. In surgery they basically let me into the surgical field, and I could observe many cases, such as artificial vessel replacement, bypass for lower-limb varicose veins and dialysis shunt creation. Since there is a doctor helicopter, I accompanied an emergency operation for a ruptured aortic aneurysm from the helipad all the way to the operating room, which was my first experience and exciting.

When entering surgery, a nurse helps you put on the surgical attire, but they said things like "Are you okay? Not too hot? Did you eat properly? Tell me if anything happens," and when I touched the unclean area with the gown and had to put it on again, in a situation where I would probably be scolded at Nagoya University, they said with a smile, "Don't worry about it!" The people of Norway were all truly full of kindness. In the second and third months, orthopedic surgery and gastrointestinal surgery had about 30 doctors, the morning conference was in a big room, and there were several residents, so every day I followed someone and was taught. They said, "Honestly, just watching outpatient clinics and chart writing is boring, isn't it? I know because I was the same," and searched for patients who could speak English, made appointments and let me actually take histories. I was able to make use of the practice from the pre-departure training at Nagoya University. In addition, I was allowed to do more and more procedures that even I seemed able to do, such as blood pressure measurement, rectal examination and simple endoscope operation.

When I arrived at the end of March it was snowing and the ground was frozen, and the temperature was around -2/3℃. It was the time heading toward spring and I avoided the severe cold of around -10℃ in December, so it was not as cold as I had imagined. The climate felt unstable: in mid-April it suddenly exceeded 20℃ and I went out in short sleeves, and the following week it was snowing again and below freezing, and I went back to a life of coats and boots. From there it gradually became warmer, but even in June the average temperature was around 12-17℃ and, without humidity, it was comfortable.

One of the things that Northern Europe is known for: I had been looking forward to life under the midnight sun a great deal before going, but it turned out to be unexpectedly stressful. When I had just arrived my sense of time went off and I could not sleep, and when I did not know how to kill time on idle evenings, it was light all the time and I felt the day would never end, and there were times I willed, "Please, sun, set soon." June had the longest days, it was light even past midnight, and the sun rose at 3. On the positive side, since it does not get dark even late, I could go out at night with peace of mind even as a woman alone, and I could feel the gratitude of the sun setting. This feeling cannot be felt unless you live in Norway.

The consumption tax rate is the second highest in the world, an astonishing 25%. At first, a bottle of water was about 300 yen even at the supermarket and 500 to 600 yen at the airport, one trip of shopping at the supermarket exceeded 7000 yen even for one person, and a hamburger was 2000 yen, and I hated how expensive everything was, but eventually I got used to it and gave up. The dormitory had a large kitchen and a full set of appliances, so I cooked for myself every day, including my lunchbox. Besides high prices, Norwegians reportedly do not like going out much because of the severe cold, value family, and like eating at home in the first place, so the restaurant industry is not developed. Instead, it has the highest consumption rate of frozen pizza in the world, and in the supermarket's frozen section one whole lane is pizza. Conversely, everyone thinks "Norway = salmon," but because of the high prices in the first place, the price is no different from eating it in Japan, so "Norway = pizza" is the right one. Public safety is quite good. Because of the high overall standard of living, there are really few homeless people, and thanks also to the midnight sun mentioned above, I never felt scared even as a woman alone.

After the weekday clerkship ended, I studied in the library and went to the gym in the dormitory to work out. The dormitory runs about five gyms, and group lessons such as dance and yoga are held every day, all in Norwegian, so at first I could not keep up at all and was embarrassed to be the only one behind the music, but eventually I came to understand simple Norwegian and it became a good break. On three-day weekends and over the Easter holidays, I went to Oslo and Bergen within Norway and also to other European countries such as Croatia and the Czech Republic, which was the best refreshment for me, who love traveling.

What I thought through studying abroad is that "living overseas does not have as high a hurdle as I expected." If it is just to "go," I think anyone can do it, as long as they have the decisiveness to go abroad in the first place. What was difficult was, in an It's up to you environment where you can do anything depending on yourself and don't have to do it if you don't want to, what to choose and how to act. Study abroad reports mainly contain the good and enjoyable aspects, so the unpleasant and hard things are hard to see, but I often agonized over things like whether there was any meaning in going every day in April to a conference in Norwegian that I understood nothing of, whether, even though it was explained to me in English, I would honestly gain more knowledge by studying in Japanese, and "what I had come to study abroad for, and that I was not living a sparkling life like the seniors I had read about in the reports." Even so, at the end of the first month, the doctors said at the conference, "Without knowing the language, you worked hard on your own," and for the first time I felt the worth of having come to study abroad. In Japan I had lived every day going to the polyclinic at the time I was told, studying for the national exam, chased by time and anxious, but in Norway, strolling the beautiful streets without doing anything in particular, and spending time with doctors who even during conferences, coffee and sweets in hand, sometimes chatted and laughed, I gained leeway in my heart. The natural environment is harsh, and the number of restaurants, the variety at supermarkets and the number of buses are all fewer than in Japan, which may be inconvenient, but the richness of heart that is said to be the reason it is at the top of the world happiness rankings was everywhere as a matter of course. From next year I will be chased by work as a resident, but if I can keep even a little of the mental leeway I gained in Norway and strive to take the kind and careful histories that the Norwegian doctors do, I think I will have gained from this study abroad more than medical knowledge and English ability. Finally, I would like to take this opportunity to express my gratitude to Dr. 粕谷 and Dr. 長谷川 and all the members of the International Collaboration Office and the Frontier Society, and everyone at the Norwegian University of Science and Technology, who gave me this valuable opportunity. Thank you very much.
